en: The Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation (from the *Tanjichōngshū*, Second Collection, Volume 23).
Authored by Jin Ruirui Shengtàn of Gusu. The Sahā World is presided over by Śākyamuni Buddha;
the Flower Treasury World (*Huàzàng shìjiè*) is presided over by Vairocana Buddha. Śākyamuni...
The Honored One has newly attained Buddhahood; Vairocana is the Buddha who attained it originally.
In other worlds, there is Amitābha Buddha, who dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. A single flower and a single world-honored one are beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

Therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* is a sūtra spoken ex cathedra without being requested; while its title begins with "The Buddha Spoke the Amitābha [Sūtra]," the word "Buddha" (佛) cannot be added below it.
Dīpaṃkara Buddha is a Buddha of a single atom; Śākyamuni Buddha is a Buddha of immeasurable atoms.
Śākyamuni Buddha is named "Healer of Illness," while Amitābha is named "Primordial Absence of Illness.
When the World-Honored One preached the *Amitābha Sūtra*, it was another provisional arrangement distinct from other sūtras, intended for the ultimate benefit of all sentient beings.

Because it cannot refute me, you have arbitrarily cited the entire Dharma-realm to say that you originally dwell within the land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), each born by transformation from a lotus flower;
what could be more excellent than this? It is like an ugly woman who, though kept in a secluded chamber or deep palace, still considers herself to be of distinguished appearance.
Among the four characters for emotion—joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—pleasure is the ultimate.
Those who know this are scholars; those who love it are sages; and those who delight in it are none other than Heaven and Earth.

As for the lotus, it is called "lian" (lotus) because it signifies the meaning of continuous connection—(the three periods of time are connected, and the flower has a calyx, and the calyx has a stalk). Because it is not the ultimate reality, it is called a "flower. Each and every sentient being sits upon a single flower;
when the flower opens and one beholds the Buddha, one beholds Śākyamuni Buddha. This is the nine grades of transformation in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding those born in the highest of the high grades: this refers to Maitreya, who is currently in his final birth before attaining Buddhahood and will achieve enlightenment here.
Regarding those born in the lowest of the low grades: these are sinners from the great Avīci Hell who will achieve Buddhahood here.

Because such persons have committed extremely evil and grave offenses, they fall into the Avīci Hell; yet there, through various causes and conditions, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) chants the name of Amitābha.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Just as a thousand-year-old dark room is illuminated by a single lamp, when these sinners hear this name, the hell itself becomes a lotus flower;
this lotus flower is within the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and this Land of Ultimate Bliss is within the world-system of Amitābha Buddha; and this world-system of Amitābha Buddha is...

Within the eight consciousnesses of a single sinner inside the immeasurable great hells—though this person has committed all manner of most heinous and grave offenses—they cannot withstand the name of Amitābha; consequently, the hells are instantly pulverized.
This is called the lowest grade of the lowest birth.
A bodhisattva does not wish to dwell in a world of defilement and turbidity; thus, they must inevitably seek rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
However, attaining rebirth in Sukhāvatī is a resultant matter. One who wishes to obtain the result must first create the cause. How does one create the cause?
This is the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Regarding the method of mindfulness of the Buddha:

one must not use a deluded mind to mindfully contemplate a distant Buddha, nor should one use a deluded mind to mindfully contemplate the deluded mind itself. Why is this? Because the deluded mind is the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);

it cannot bring about resonance or communication with the primordial limit (*mūla-koṭi*). Since it cannot bring about resonance or communication due to being the cause of birth and death, the Buddha is fundamentally not...
It is remote, and thus becomes increasingly remote. Furthermore, regarding the deluded mind contemplating the deluded mind:
ordinary beings are precisely sustained by their deluded minds until they fall into hell. Now, one further teaches them to practice such mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

They then take the preceding deluded mind as the object of mindfulness and the subsequent deluded mind as the Buddha; or alternatively, they take the preceding deluded mind as the Buddha and the subsequent deluded mind as the mindfulness. As it is said:
This is no different from wandering through the mundane world. Therefore, this method is not to be employed.

As for the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*), one should not first visualize the Buddha and then perform the recollection; rather, one should first complete the recollection and then see the Buddha.
Why is this so? If one visualizes the Buddha first, what is the status of that Buddha? One who acts thus is called a person of great falsehood. Furthermore, it is...
To cause the way of resonance and response to intersect, the Buddha may manifest; yet, by the time the Buddha arrives, the one who was mindful of him has long since departed.
Moreover, that which is capable of mindfulness is precisely the deluded mind. How can this deluded mind presume to encounter the Buddha abruptly?

As for the claim that one first achieves mindfulness and subsequently sees the Buddha, it implies that the mindfulness is real while the Buddha is merely provisional. The Bodhisattva takes the ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) as the object of mindfulness, yet uses the deluded mind [to do so].

[Question: Why does one not take the deluded mind as the object of mindfulness? [Answer: Because the primordial limit (*koṭi*) is the Buddha. [Question: Why? [Answer: The primordial limit cannot be seen.
That which cannot be seen cannot cause a practitioner to give rise to a heart of joy. Furthermore, in the primordial limit, not even a speck of dust can be established.
If a practitioner exerts effort regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it would be a great contradiction. Also, using lion’s milk for glass...

It is held in a crystal bowl; other vessels cannot contain it. If a practitioner seeks the primordial limit with a deluded mind, it is like placing lion’s milk in a poisoned vessel—it will ultimately not be received.
Furthermore, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi stands in opposition to birth and death;
if one pursues it with a deluded mind, there is no doubt that one will eventually enter the ocean of birth and death. (End)
